common_name: Bugle Butternut Squash (Compact Powdery Mildew-Resistant Butternut)

planting.note: Direct sow in warm soil after frost; Bugle is a Cornell-bred butternut selected for strong powdery mildew resistance on a more compact vine than older butternut varieties, letting the foliage stay productive later into a humid Gulf South summer.

directions: Sow seed directly in warm soil after all danger of frost, allowing the vines room to spread; Bugle is a butternut squash bred at Cornell University with strong resistance to powdery mildew, the fungal disease that typically coats squash foliage in a white film and shuts down photosynthesis well before fruit has finished sizing and curing in humid Southern gardens. Because the leaf canopy stays healthier longer, Bugle tends to fill out a fuller crop of the classic tan, elongated-neck fruit with dense, sweet orange flesh than mildew-susceptible butternut varieties planted in the same conditions. Let the squash mature fully to a hard rind before harvest, then cure in a warm, dry spot for one to two weeks; properly cured fruit stores for several months and is excellent roasted, baked, or pureed into soup.
sources: seed catalog reference (Rupp Seeds, True Leaf Market)

planting.note: Direct sow in warm soil after frost; Metro PMR was bred jointly by Cornell University and a commercial seed company specifically for high powdery mildew resistance, an important trait for keeping butternut vines productive through the humid second half of a Gulf South growing season.

directions: Sow seed directly in warm soil after all danger of frost, allowing the vines room to spread; Metro PMR is a butternut squash hybrid bred specifically for high resistance to powdery mildew, so foliage stays greener and more productive later into summer than standard butternut varieties, which typically succumb to mildew before the crop has fully sized and cured. It produces the classic tan, bottle-shaped butternut fruit with dense, sweet, deep orange flesh well suited to roasting, soups, and purees. Let fruit mature fully to a hard rind before harvest, then cure in a warm, dry, well-ventilated spot for one to two weeks; properly cured squash stores for several months in a cool, dry pantry.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Divergent is a galia-cantaloupe cross bred for high resistance to Fusarium wilt races 0-2 and intermediate powdery mildew resistance, a strong disease package for humid Gulf South melon growing.

directions: Direct sow in warm soil, thinning to 2 plants per hill spaced 3-4 feet apart; Divergent is a galia-type melon crossed with cantaloupe genetics, bred for high resistance to Fusarium wilt (a soil-borne fungal disease that can persist in garden soil for years) along with intermediate resistance to powdery mildew, making it a resilient choice for gardens where melons have struggled with disease in the past. The smaller, aromatic fruit has the sweet, floral flavor typical of galia melons with the familiar netted rind of a cantaloupe, ripening earlier than many standard cantaloupe varieties. Harvest when the skin turns from green to golden-tan under the netting and the fruit slips easily from the vine with a fragrant aroma at the stem end. Because it is an organic-bred hybrid popular with market growers, it performs well under lower-input, disease-conscious growing conditions.
sources: seed catalog reference (High Mowing Organic Seeds, Territorial Seed)

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date. Karma is a blocky bell pepper hybrid bred with resistance to common mosaic viruses, which spread readily through aphid activity in warm Gulf South gardens.

directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date; Karma is a hybrid bell pepper bred with resistance to common mosaic viruses, letting it keep its foliage healthier through the aphid pressure that builds over a long, warm Gulf South growing season. It produces large, thick-walled, blocky green bells that ripen to red with good sweetness if left on the plant longer. The compact, well-branched plant provides good leaf cover that helps shield developing fruit from sunscald during peak summer heat. Harvest at the green stage for a milder flavor or let fruit fully ripen to red for maximum sweetness, and keep picking to encourage continued fruit set.
sources: seed catalog reference (Tomato Growers Supply Company)

common_name: Revolution Bell Pepper (Bacterial Spot and Phytophthora-Resistant Hybrid)

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date. Revolution carries resistance to multiple races of bacterial leaf spot, cucumber mosaic virus, and Phytophthora root rot — a broad disease package well matched to the wet, humid disease pressure of Gulf South summers.

directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date; Revolution is a bell pepper hybrid bred for an unusually broad disease package, combining resistance to several races of bacterial leaf spot with tolerance to cucumber mosaic virus and Phytophthora root rot, a soil-borne disease that thrives in the heavy rain and poorly drained spots common in Gulf Coast gardens. It produces large, thick-walled, blocky green bells that ripen to red with good sweetness if left on the plant. Because it resists both a major foliar disease and a major root disease, Revolution tends to hold up better than many varieties through a wet, humid growing season. Harvest at the green stage for milder flavor or allow fruit to fully ripen to red, and keep picking regularly to encourage continued production.
sources: seed catalog reference (Tomato Growers Supply Company, Holmes Seed Company)
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pepper Production
